review-neurips-2026-139438.title: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning

checks.claim: Every feasible instance has an optimal finite-threshold selector.
checks.explanation: Full acceptance maximizes coverage whenever the budgets permit it. If the mixed uncertainty score is unbounded, no finite threshold represents that optimum. Appendix A divides by a combination of nonnegative multipliers without first handling the case in which both multipliers vanish.
checks.demonstration:
Use squared loss $\ell(\widehat y,y)=(\widehat y-y)^2$ and a Bayesian model with $X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, parameter $\theta$ equally likely to be $-1$ or $1$, and response $Y=(\theta+\eta)\sqrt X$, where the noise sign $\eta$ is independent and equally likely to be $-1$ or $1$.

Take one training pair $(X_0,Y_0)$ with the same parameter and an independent noise sign. Conditional on either parameter value and any $X_0=x_0>0$, the observation $Y_0=0$ has probability $1/2$. A dataset $\mathcal D=\{(x_0,0)\}$ therefore leaves the parameter posterior uniform. The event $Y_0=0$ itself has positive probability; no positive mass is required at a single continuous input value.

The known-parameter Bayes predictor is $h(x,\theta)=\theta\sqrt x$, while the posterior Bayes predictor is $H(x,\mathcal D)=0$. Averaging squared loss over the posterior parameter and new noise, as in Definition 1, gives

$$A^*(x)=x,\qquad E^*(x)=x,\qquad T^*(x)=2x.$$

These scores are integrable. Every mixture $(1-\lambda)A^*(X)+\lambda E^*(X)$ equals $X$ and has a continuous distribution, including both endpoints $\lambda=1/2$ and $\lambda=1$. The theorem’s assumptions are satisfied.

In $(\mathrm P_\rho)$, choose risk budget $b=3$ and regret budget $g=2$. The selector $C\equiv1$ has coverage $1$, risk $2$, and regret $1$. It is feasible and is the unique coverage maximizer up to null sets, because $0\le C\le1$ and $\mathbb E C=1$ force $C=1$ almost surely. Every finite threshold instead gives

$$\Pr(X\le\tau)=\begin{cases}0,&\tau<0,\\1-e^{-\tau},&\tau\ge0,\end{cases}$$

which is strictly less than $1$. Both constraints are slack at the optimum, so complementary slackness forces their multipliers $\alpha=\beta=0$. Appendix A’s formulas divide by $2\alpha+\beta=0$. Appendix B’s allowance for a shifted operating threshold does not introduce $\tau=+\infty$ or handle the corresponding zero-coefficient case.
checks.repair:
Add the full-acceptance branch to the coverage problem: if $\mathbb E T^*(X)\le b$ and $\mathbb E E^*(X)\le g$, take $C\equiv1$. Equivalently, permit $\tau=+\infty$ in the theorem. Otherwise use the finite-threshold branch. This covers every instance of $(\mathrm P_\rho)$ under its stated positive budgets, integrability and continuity assumptions.

For completeness, let $\mu$ be the input distribution. The set of measurable selectors $0\le C\le1$ is weak-star compact in $L^\infty(\mu)$. Integration against $1$, $T^*$ and $E^*$ is weak-star continuous because these functions belong to $L^1(\mu)$. The feasible set is therefore compact and an optimum exists. Positive budgets make $C=0$ strictly feasible for both budget inequalities. Convex separation, or Slater duality with the box $0\le C\le1$ as the domain, gives finite multipliers $\alpha,\beta\ge0$ and the Lagrangian

$$\mathcal L(C)=\mathbb E\!\left[C(X)\{-1+\alpha A^*(X)+(\alpha+\beta)E^*(X)\}\right]-\alpha b-\beta g.$$

If full acceptance is infeasible, both multipliers cannot be zero: minimizing $-\mathbb E C$ over the box would otherwise require $C\equiv1$. Thus $2\alpha+\beta>0$. Pointwise minimization gives the finite-threshold selector with

$$\lambda=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2\alpha+\beta}\in[1/2,1],\qquad \tau=\frac1{2\alpha+\beta}.$$

The assumed continuous distribution of this mixed score makes the threshold tie set null. State the full-acceptance branch before dividing in Appendix A, and handle zero coefficients before the analogous division in Appendix B. This supplies the missing coverage boundary; no additional proof of the separate risk- or regret-minimization branches is asserted.
checks.scope: The gap is the full-acceptance boundary of the coverage problem $(\mathrm P_\rho)$ in Equation (7), Theorem 1 and Appendix A, Case 1. Adding this branch completes the coverage result; when the budgets exclude full acceptance, the usual finite-threshold form is valid. This counterexample does not assess the separate risk- or regret-minimization branches.
checks.claimContext: For a fixed training dataset $\mathcal D$, write $A^*(x)$, $E^*(x)$ and $T^*(x)=A^*(x)+E^*(x)$ for the aleatoric, epistemic and total expected losses. Equation (7), denoted $(\mathrm P_\rho)$, maximizes the coverage $\rho(C)=\mathbb E C(X)$ over selectors $0\le C\le1$, subject to $Ri(C)=\mathbb E[C(X)T^*(X)]\le b$ and $Re(C)=\mathbb E[C(X)E^*(X)]\le g$, with positive budgets $b,g$. Theorem 1 states that every feasible instance has an optimum of the following form with $\lambda\in[1/2,1]$ and finite $\tau\in\mathbb R$.
checks.whyItMatters: The theorem claims attainment by a finite threshold for every feasible coverage problem. When all inputs may be accepted, finite thresholds can approach the optimal coverage without attaining it.

checks.claim: Normalized and unnormalized risk/regret formulations have identical optimal selectors.
checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. The proposed example compares optimizers at unchanged numerical budgets and finds different thresholds. Appendix B already states that normalization can shift the optimal operating threshold. Read with that qualification, the Section 3 remark concerns the common selector family. A change in the cutoff does not contradict this contextual claim.
checks.demonstration:
The relevant qualification appears in the final paragraph of Appendix B, p. 16. It says that normalization "purely shifts the optimal operating threshold" $\tau$ and that the "functional form of the boundary" remains identical. Theorem 1 likewise describes an existential threshold form for each feasible optimization instance; it does not assign one common numerical cutoff to all such instances.

The proposed construction is mathematically valid. Let $X\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$, let the parameter $\theta$ and noise $\varepsilon$ be independent uniform signs, and set $Y=(\theta+\varepsilon)\sqrt X$ under squared loss. One training observation with the same parameter and independent noise has $Y_0=0$ with probability $1/2$, leaving the posterior on $\theta$ uniform. The known-parameter predictor is $h(x,\theta)=\theta\sqrt x$, the posterior Bayes predictor is $H(x,\mathcal D)=0$, and the uncertainty components satisfy

$$A^*(x)=E^*(x)=x,\qquad T^*(x)=2x.$$

Every score $(1-\lambda)A^*(X)+\lambda E^*(X)$ required by Theorem 1 equals the continuously distributed $X$. For any measurable, possibly randomized selector $C$ of positive coverage $c$, comparison with $C_c(x)=\mathbf1_{[0,c]}(x)$ gives

$$\int_0^1(x-c)\bigl(C(x)-C_c(x)\bigr)\,dx\ge0,$$

and hence $Ri(C)\ge c^2$ and $SRi(C)\ge c$, with equality for $C_c$. At risk budget $1/2$ and inactive regret budget $2$, the optimal coverages are therefore $1/\sqrt2$ before normalization and $1/2$ after normalization.

Both optimizing selectors threshold the same score $X$; their cutoffs differ. This is the threshold shift that Appendix B expressly permits. The calculation does not refute the assigned statement when read with that qualification, and it does not test the separate assertion about identifying numerical Lagrange multipliers across optimization problems.
checks.scope: Section 3 and Appendix B explicitly allow the threshold to shift when the normalization changes. The fixed-budget construction illustrates behavior already allowed by that qualification. It neither validates Theorem 1 in full nor establishes a separate error in the appendix's multiplier calculation.
checks.title: Appendix B allows the optimal threshold to change under normalization
checks.whyItMatters: The comparison separates equality of a selector family from equality of its operating thresholds. Appendix B already makes that distinction, so the fixed-budget calculation does not establish a mathematical error in the assigned claim.
checks.claimContext: Section 3 defines coverage $\rho(C)$, accepted risk $Ri(C)$ and accepted regret $Re(C)$ for a selector $C:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. Its remark says that normalization gives the same optimal solution set and refers to Appendix B. The appendix explicitly allows the optimal threshold $\tau$ to shift, while stating that the selector's functional form and range $\lambda\in[1/2,1]$ remain the same.

checks.location: Section 2.4, comparison of Barker and MH asymptotic variance
checks.claim: Barker asymptotic variance is at most twice MH asymptotic variance.
checks.explanation: The cited result also includes the stationary variance of the observable. Dropping that additive term gives a false multiplicative guarantee, even for a standard Gaussian target with an independent exact-target proposal.
checks.demonstration:
Let the target be $p=\mathcal N(0,1)$ and propose independently from $q(y\mid x)=p(y)$. The acceptance ratio is identically one. MH therefore gives independent samples, whereas Barker accepts each independent proposal with probability $1/2$ and otherwise keeps the current state. For $f(x)=x$, the stationary variance is one and Barker’s lag-$k$ covariance is $2^{-k}$. Consequently,
$$\sigma_{f,\mathrm{MH}}^2=1,\qquad\sigma_{f,B}^2=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}=3>2.$$
Both chains have the correct target and a finite central-limit variance.
checks.repair:
State the cited theorem with its additive term:
$$\sigma_{f,\mathrm{MH}}^2\le\sigma_{f,B}^2\le2\sigma_{f,\mathrm{MH}}^2+\operatorname{Var}_p(f).$$
Indeed, the half-lazy MH kernel $P_{1/2}=(I+P_{\mathrm{MH}})/2$ accepts half as often as MH. Barker accepts at least as often as this kernel and no more often than MH, so Peskun ordering places its asymptotic variance between theirs. The spectral identity for the half-lazy kernel gives $\sigma_{f,P_{1/2}}^2=2\sigma_{f,\mathrm{MH}}^2+\operatorname{Var}_p(f)$, which proves the displayed comparison under the cited reversible-chain central-limit assumptions.

checks.demonstration:
For any $u\in(0,1)$, choose $s=\sigma(T\operatorname{logit}(u))$. Substitution gives

$$f_T(s)=\sigma\!\left(\frac{T\operatorname{logit}(u)}{T}\right)=u.$$

Thus every interior probability remains attainable. In particular, $s=\sigma(T)$ gives $f_T(s)=\sigma(1)\approx0.7311$, which exceeds the stated upper endpoint. Taking the limits $s\downarrow0$ and $s\uparrow1$ gives the two endpoints.
checks.repair:
Describe the range of the actual evaluated inputs, or state an explicit clipping convention. If $s$ is clipped to $[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$, the range becomes

$$\left[\sigma\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{logit}(\varepsilon)}T\right),\sigma\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{logit}(1-\varepsilon)}T\right)\right].$$

For $T=47.9$ and $\varepsilon=10^{-10}$, this is approximately $[0.382,0.618]$. That calculation explains the quoted band under an added clipping convention; the formula printed in the paper does not include one.
checks.scope: The error is in the description of the transformation’s range. Strict monotonicity still preserves ranking on the unclipped interior. Explicit clipping can create ties, so its effect on ranking depends on the input values.

checks.demonstration: Use one binary feature $x\in\{0,1\}$ and split the root into $x=0$ and $x=1$. Alternatively, restrict the always-adjacent assertion to continuous closed halfspace splits in a convex parent region: a segment joining points in the two children crosses their common split hyperplane, proving activity on both sides. Binary splits need a separate definition.

checks.claim: Bregman projection equals local update for general regularizers.
checks.explanation: At a boundary optimum, the score vector and the regularizer gradient differ by a normal-cone term as well as a constant simplex multiplier. That term need not be constant on the selected face. Dropping it changes the local minimizer.
checks.demonstration:
Use three feasible outputs $e_1,e_2,e_3$, scores $s=(1,4/5,0)$ and $\Omega(p)=\tfrac12\|p\|_2^2$. The global simplex optimum is $p=(3/5,2/5,0)$. Freeze the first output coordinate at zero, leaving the local face supported on outputs $2,3$.

The local regularized update projects $(4/5,0)$ onto the two-coordinate simplex, giving $(9/10,1/10)$. The Bregman divergence is squared Euclidean distance, so projecting the global vector onto the same face instead gives $(7/10,3/10)$. These are different. The global face has probability $2/5$, so its Gibbs conditional is well-defined. Adding a constant to normalize the regularizer at vertices does not change the example.
checks.repair:
For a differentiable regularizer and an interior global optimum, the KKT identity is $\nabla\Omega(p)=s-\nu\mathbf1$, and the stated Bregman argument is valid. To include boundary optima, retain the nonnegativity multipliers. An exact alternative minimizes the Fenchel–Young gap

$$L_\Omega(\iota_k q,s)=\Omega(\iota_k q)+\Omega^*(s)-s^\top\iota_k q.$$

Here $\Omega^*$ is the convex conjugate of the regularizer on the simplex. Its value is constant during the minimization over $q$, so this gives precisely the local regularized update, including at boundary optima. It changes the general geometric identity; it does not make the Bregman-only formula true. For nonsmooth regularizers, a gradient-based divergence also needs an appropriate definition or stronger regularity assumptions.
checks.scope: The general Bregman-projection identification fails for a permitted sparse quadratic optimum. The exact Fenchel–Young replacement preserves the local optimization but changes its geometric characterization. The entropy/Gibbs case and the algorithm’s measured results are not contradicted by this example.
checks.claimContext: Appendix A.1 identifies a local regularized update with the Bregman projection of the global optimum $p_\Omega(s)$ onto a simplex face. Here $s$ is the vector of scores, $\Omega$ the regularizer, and $\iota_k$ embeds a local probability vector into the full simplex. The assumptions allow quadratic regularization and sparse global optima.
checks.title: A boundary optimum invalidates the general Bregman-projection identity
checks.whyItMatters: A geometric interpretation used for later bias bounds must remain valid when the regularizer assigns zero probability to some feasible outputs.

checks.claim: Cut-bound holds for perturbation noise of Definition 3.5.
checks.explanation: A product feasible set does not imply independent block maximizers when the perturbation coordinates are dependent. The cut-only right-hand side can be zero even though the global conditional distribution differs from the local update.
checks.demonstration:
Take $\mathcal Y=\{0,1\}^2$, zero scores and perturbation scale one. Let $Z$ be a centered bivariate Gaussian with unit variances and correlation $\rho=1/2$. Its density is strictly positive everywhere, as required by the general noise definition. The global maximizer is $(\mathbf1\{Z_1>0\},\mathbf1\{Z_2>0\})$.

Freeze the first bit at one. A local update of the second bit uses its marginal noise and selects one with probability $1/2$. The global conditional probability is instead

$$\Pr(Z_2>0\mid Z_1>0)=\frac12+\frac{\arcsin\rho}{\pi}=\frac23.$$

Their TV distance is $1/6$. There are no cut constraints for this product feasible set, so the proposed bound is zero. The additional independence condition in the earlier product-space result is not supplied by the positive-density assumption.
checks.repair:
State and verify block independence when invoking product-space exactness. For a general noise law, retain the dependence and conditioning terms. Let $e$ be the probability that the relaxed free optimum violates the fixed boundary, $\beta$ the probability that the global relaxed optimum is infeasible, and $p>0$ the probability of the frozen assignment under the constrained global law. Let $d$ be the TV distance between the relaxed free marginal and its conditional law at that assignment. Common-noise coupling and triangle inequality give the valid bound

$$\operatorname{TV}(q_{\mathrm{local}},q_{\mathrm{global}\mid S})\le e+d+\frac{2\beta}{p},$$

provided both conditioning probabilities are positive. This bound includes dependence and rare-conditioning effects; it does not establish the original cut-only expression.
checks.scope: The cut-only bound is false for the stated general positive-density noise class. The correlated-noise example does not refute a version restricted to independent perturbations. That restriction also needs a valid conditioning argument: equality of two unconditioned optimizers on a feasibility event does not by itself bound their differently conditioned laws by the same local violation probability. The broader correction includes the missing dependence and conditioning effects.
checks.claimContext: Definition 3.5 permits perturbation noise with a positive joint density. The cut-bound proposition bounds the local consistency gap $\delta_{\theta,\Omega_\varepsilon}$ by violations of constraints connecting frozen coordinates $S$ to free coordinates $F$. Here $Y^*_{\mathrm{relax}}$ maximizes the perturbed score after those cut constraints are removed, and $V_c(S,y)$ is the set of free assignments violating cut constraint $c$ at frozen assignment $y_S$. The preceding product-space proposition separately assumes independent noise blocks.
checks.title: A cut-only bias bound misses dependence in the perturbation noise
checks.whyItMatters: Variables can be statistically dependent through the perturbations even without a constraint connecting them. A constraint graph alone cannot measure that dependence.

Let the local advantages have zero mean. Expanding the square gives
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(n^{-1/2}\sum_i A_i\right)=n^{-1}\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(A_i)+2n^{-1}\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(A_i,A_j).$$
The ideal unit-variance case has variance one only when the sum of cross-covariances vanishes. An admissible reward construction assigns the same nonconstant rollout score to each principle. checks.demonstration:
For a general control, the entropy gap is
\[H(\pi^u)-\mathcal L_{\rm ENT}(u)=\mathbb E_{X_1}D_{\rm KL}(\Pi^u_{|1}\|\Pi^0_{|1})\]
The path-space KL chain rule separates a terminal-marginal KL from the expected conditional-bridge KL. For a fixed terminal marginal, the latter is nonnegative and minimized at zero by using the reference bridges. The exact stochastic-control optimizer specified in Section 4.2 therefore belongs to that reciprocal class, as Remark B.1 describes. review-neurips-2026-151296.title: CausalBind: Causal Modeling and Learning for Protein-Molecule Virtual Screening

checks.location: Appendix A4.5.3, proof of Theorem 2, Step 3, 'Lemma 1 (Antichain recovery)'
checks.claim: For any antichain 0/1 interaction mask M, the only invertible A,B satisfying M~ = A M B on supp(M~) are (permutation) x (positive diagonal) matrices, which is used to conclude the reparameterization Jacobians J_F, J_G are diagonal up to permutation.
checks.explanation: An identity interaction mask remains unchanged under matching orthogonal changes of coordinates in both modalities. This ambiguity preserves the full observed distribution and satisfies the theorem's variability condition. The error therefore reaches the component-wise conclusion of Theorem 2, beyond the false matrix lemma.
checks.demonstration:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let the two latent modality vectors $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ be independent standard Gaussians, let both observation maps be the identity, and choose the binary mask $\mathcal M=I_d$ and compatibility function $\phi(a,b)=ab$. The binding probability is then $\sigma(x^\top y)$, where $\sigma(t)=(1+e^{-t})^{-1}$. Every row and column of the mask has a singleton support, so both support families are antichains. There are only $d$ nonzero entries among $d^2$, and the density $1/d$ can be made arbitrarily small.

Let $R$ act as the identity after coordinate two and have first block
$$R_{1:2,1:2}=\begin{pmatrix}3/5&4/5\\-4/5&3/5\end{pmatrix}.$$
Define alternative concepts $\tilde x=Rx$ and $\tilde y=Ry$, use $R^\top$ as both alternative observation maps, and keep the same mask, compatibility function and priors. Orthogonality gives
$$(Rx)^\top(Ry)=x^\top y,\qquad R^\top\tilde x=x,\qquad R^\top\tilde y=y.$$
The standard-Gaussian priors, their independence and the observed variables are therefore unchanged, as is the binding probability. In particular, the entire binder-selected observed distribution is identical. Both observation maps are invertible; deterministic nuisance variables are allowed. All coordinates remain active, every open latent set has positive selected density, and symmetry gives $\Pr(B=1)=1/2$.

The finite-probe condition also holds. Write $Z(x)=\int p(y)\sigma(x^\top y)\,dy$ and
$$\eta(y;x)=\log p(y)+\log\sigma(x^\top y)-\log Z(x).$$
Its mixed derivative matrix is
$$V(x,y)=(1-s)I_d-s(1-s)yx^\top,\qquad s=\sigma(x^\top y).$$
Use the $d$ probes $x=e_r$, where $e_r$ is the $r$th coordinate vector, and evaluate at $y=\mathbf1$. For each $j$, select the off-diagonal matrix entry $(1+(j\bmod d),j)$. Across the probes, these entries form the response minor
$$-\sigma(1)(1-\sigma(1))I_d.$$
Its determinant is nonzero, so the $d$ vector-valued response functions are linearly independent. Continuity and the strictly positive selected density give the required almost-everywhere functional independence. The same calculation applies in the alternative coordinates because their model has exactly the same form. For the numerical choice $d=128$, the mask has $128$ nonzeros, density $0.0078125$, and the minor has rank $128$.

Yet each of the first two alternative coordinates depends on two original coordinates. Thus the representations are not related by a permutation followed by componentwise maps, contradicting individual-concept identifiability under the stated hypotheses. This example preserves the mask support exactly; it does not assert that two different supports are observationally equivalent. The supporting antichain lemma fails directly as well: $A=R$ and $B=R^\top$ satisfy $A I_d B=I_d$, although neither is a product of a permutation and a positive diagonal matrix.
checks.repair: A theorem recovering individual concepts needs additional assumptions that exclude the joint coordinate changes $(x,y)\mapsto(Rx,Ry)$, followed by an identification proof using those assumptions. Sparsity, antichain support, Gaussian coordinate independence and the current finite-probe condition all hold in this example, so strengthening the argument without changing those premises cannot recover the stated conclusion. Enlarging the equivalence class to include joint orthogonal changes would avoid this particular contradiction, but would weaken individual-concept recovery; no full replacement theorem follows from that change alone.
checks.scope: The contradiction concerns the componentwise latent-concept conclusion of Theorem 2 and its antichain-recovery lemma. The example preserves the mask support, so it does not separately refute support recovery.
checks.title: Sparse antichains do not identify individual latent concepts
checks.whyItMatters: The same binder-selected observations can correspond to different mixtures of the supposed atomic concepts, even when the interaction mask is fixed and very sparse. Theorem 2 consequently does not justify recovery of individual concepts under its stated assumptions.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 2 claims component-wise identifiability from binder-selected observations under sparse antichain support and finite-probe variability. Its proof uses an antichain-recovery lemma to rule out linear mixing of the latent concepts.
checks.checkedLocation: Definition 1; Assumptions 1–3; Theorem 2, Conditions 2.i–ii; Appendix A4.5.3, Lemma 1

checks.explanation: A covariance estimated from \(m\) centered observations has rank at most \(m-1\). Therefore a full nonsingular Gaussian density is not defined when the feature dimension is at least \(m\), unless an explicit regularization or dimensionality reduction is supplied.
checks.demonstration: Let the centered data matrix be \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\). Its rows sum to zero, so \(\operatorname{rank}X\le m-1\), and \(\widehat\Sigma=X^\top X/(m-1)\) has the same rank bound. With twenty observations in twenty dimensions, taking the uncentered observations as the coordinate vectors gives \(\widehat\Sigma=(I-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/20)/19\). Its product with \(\mathbf1\) is zero, so its determinant vanishes and its inverse does not exist.

review-neurips-2026-151670.plainExplanation: The printed algorithm squares its retained Gram matrix and uses a threshold floor inconsistent with the proof. The privacy analysis also confuses variance with standard deviation and does not compose its internal budgets into the headline pair. Further proof corrections concern the Gaussian fourth moment, weighted filtering, initialization dimension, truncation bias, two-sided Bernstein constants, zero-singular SVD completions, a dropped sample-gap hypothesis, an inflated intermediate success probability and a missing factor in the recurrence. These local defects have distinct scopes; they do not jointly establish failure of the final asymptotic rate.

checks.location: Main text 3.4, Proposition 2, versus Appendix A.2 conclusion
checks.claim: Joint training admits an exact one-parameter family of loss minimizers, so the cost coefficient is not identifiable.
checks.explanation: Uniform approximation of a compensating correction need not attain the same loss exactly. To disprove exact attainment, it is necessary to rule out every admissible correction at a shifted coefficient, not just the particular shifted function proposed in the proof. A balanced two-input example provides that obstruction while satisfying the proposition's abstract density and cost-recoverability assumptions.
checks.demonstration:
Take two available alternatives and foundation outputs \(q^{(1)}=(1/4,3/4)\), \(q^{(2)}=(3/4,1/4)\). At each input observe each alternative once. Set \(\mathrm{cost}_1(q)=q_1\), \(\mathrm{cost}_2(q)=0\), and all other varying structural features to zero.

Let \(\mathcal G\) be pairs of rational-coefficient polynomials on the simplex. This class is dense: continuous functions can first be approximated by real polynomials and then their finitely many coefficients by rationals.

Allow any real alternative-intercept difference \(a\). Equation (1) gives the logit
\[z(q)=\beta_{\mathrm{cost}}q_1+g_1(q)-g_2(q)+a.\]
The balanced loss at each input is
\[\ell(z)=\tfrac12\log(1+e^z)+\tfrac12\log(1+e^{-z})\geq\log2,\]
with equality exactly at \(z=0\). Thus the empirical loss reaches \(L^*=\log2\) exactly when both logits vanish. A minimizer exists at \(\beta_{\mathrm{cost}}=-1\), \(g_1(q)=q_1\), \(g_2=0\), \(a=0\), respecting the negative coefficient constraint.

Every admissible polynomial has rational values at both rational inputs. Subtracting the two zero-logit equations therefore gives
\[0=z(q^{(2)})-z(q^{(1)})=\tfrac12\beta_{\mathrm{cost}}+r,\qquad r\in\mathbb Q.\]
Hence an irrational cost coefficient cannot attain the minimum with any correction in the class, even if the intercept changes freely. Every sign-preserving open interval contains such coefficients, so no asserted interval of exact minimizers exists. Nevertheless, rational linear corrections can approach the compensating slope arbitrarily closely, giving infimum \(\log2\) for every negative coefficient.
checks.repair:
Use the limiting conclusion already stated in Appendix A.2:
\[\inf_{g\in\mathcal G}L(\beta^{(c)},g)=L^*.\]
Indeed, continuous cost recovery makes \(g^{(0)}-c\kappa\) continuous. Density supplies a correction within \(\varepsilon\) in sup norm. The negative log-softmax is \(2\)-Lipschitz in that norm, so its empirical loss differs from \(L^*\) by at most \(2\varepsilon\); global minimality supplies the opposite inequality for the infimum.
For an exact family, add closure under the required shifts \(g\mapsto g-c\kappa\). For a finite training set, the weaker requirement of exact interpolation of those shifted utility differences at the observed foundation outputs is enough, allowing a common additive offset across alternatives at each observation. The resulting utilities have identical softmax probabilities and exactly equal loss.
checks.scope: The failure is the exact-attainment conclusion under the proposition's abstract density-only assumption. The example is not a counterexample for the implemented real-weight MLP, and it does not deny approximate non-identifiability or establish a gradient-descent trajectory.

The transported errors are \(e_1\pm\tau e_2\), so \[\Gamma^{(L)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Gamma^{(\ell),\mathrm{BP}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\tau^2\end{pmatrix}.\] Their ranks are \(1\) and \(2\). A realization using the paper’s scaled residual, LayerNorm and ReLU block also exists: with \(L=2\), normalization constant \(1\), \(a=(1,-1)^\top/\sqrt2\) and \(W=\eta ae_2^\top\) for a scale \(\eta>0\), use two positive inputs with second coordinates \(1/\eta\) and \(2/\eta\). The first component of the residual branch has derivative \[q(t)=\frac{\eta}{2\sqrt2(1+t^2/2)^{3/2}},\qquad t\in\{1,2\}.\] A squared loss with labels chosen to give output error \(e_1\) yields transported errors \((1,q(1))\) and \((1,q(2))\). Their Gram determinant is \((q(1)-q(2))^2/4>0\). The Jacobian deviations shrink with \(\eta\), so the rank mismatch is not confined to abstract matrices.

Take \(n\) equally likely samples in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), with orthonormal basis \(e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_n\). On sample \(i\), let \(\delta_i=e_i\) and \(J_i=I+a e_i e_0^\top\). The reference is \(I\), its singular values are one, and \(\|J_i-I\|_{\mathrm{op}}=a\). With \(L=2\), the residual form \(J_i=I+B_i/L\) has \(\|B_i\|_{\mathrm{op}}=2a=\bar\rho\). Thus the stated transport hypotheses hold. Since \(J_i^\top\delta_i=e_i+a e_0\), \(\Gamma\) has effective rank \(n\), while \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{BP}}\) has nonzero eigenvalues \(a^2+1/n\) once and \(1/n\) repeated \(n-1\) times. Therefore
\[\operatorname{erank}(\Gamma_{\mathrm{BP}})=\frac{(1+a^2)^2}{a^4+(1+2a^2)/n}.\]
For \(n=100000\), \(a=0.1\), and \(\bar\rho=0.2\), this is approximately \(9256.81\), below \(e^{-1.6}n\approx20189.65\).

checks.demonstration:
Choose orthonormal zero-mean vectors \(v,u_1,u_2\in\mathbb R^4\), put \(B=u_1u_1^\top+u_2u_2^\top\), and set \(G(h)=h^\top B h/2\). At depth \(\ell\), use the four equally weighted states
\[h_{\ell,j,\pm}=\sqrt{4-a_\ell^2}\,v\pm a_\ell u_j,\qquad j=1,2,\quad a_\ell=2^{-\ell}.\]
Each state is zero-mean with squared norm four, and all converge to \(2v\); their normalized kernel converges exponentially to the all-ones kernel. Yet \(\nabla G(h_{\ell,j,\pm})=\pm a_\ell u_j\). Every state has the same goodness \(a_\ell^2/2\). Assigning equal positive and negative example mass to each state makes the squared logistic weight average the same positive scalar \(b_\ell\). Therefore
\[\Gamma^{(\ell),\mathrm{FFA}}=\frac{b_\ell a_\ell^2}{2}(u_1u_1^\top+u_2u_2^\top),\qquad\operatorname{erank}(\Gamma^{(\ell),\mathrm{FFA}})=2.\]
The goodness gradient is globally Lipschitz with constant one, but its limit at \(2v\) is zero.

checks.location: Appendix A.4, inequalities22–23 and final equality; work/text/156147.txt:1104
checks.claim: The gain-matrix chain establishes Euclidean mean-update conservativity.
checks.explanation: Covariance order does not justify replacing both sides of an arbitrary matrix sandwich, and the chain’s final expression is not the Kalman gain square, leaving conservativity unproved.
checks.demonstration:
From \(\hat P\preceq\tilde P\), one cannot generally infer \(\hat P C\hat P\preceq\tilde P C\tilde P\) for an arbitrary positive-semidefinite middle matrix. For \(\hat P=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)\), \(\tilde P=I\), and \(C=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), all three matrices are positive definite and \(\hat P\preceq\tilde P\), but the difference is \(\begin{pmatrix}3/2&1/2\\1/2&0\end{pmatrix}\), with negative determinant.

Independently, in the scalar case \(\tilde P=R=H=1\), the Kalman posterior covariance and gain are \(1/2\), so its gain square is \(1/4\), whereas the claimed final expression \(\tilde P^2/R^2\) is one. This equality defect persists in the actual zero-residual optimum setting.
checks.repair: Prove the mean bound directly from the optimizer’s valid identities or provide justified commutation/structural conditions for each matrix-order step, using the actual Kalman gain expression.
checks.scope: The displayed proof chain fails. The generic matrix witness is not claimed to be an optimizer, and no counterexample to the conservativity conclusion itself is established.
